theme: The glory of God in creation and the dignity of man
settingTheScene: The Psalms are the prayer book of the Bible, the songs, laments, and praises that the people of God have prayed for three thousand years. They were sung in the Temple, prayed by Jesus on the cross, and read in the church from the beginning. This plan weaves them in alongside the historical books because the Psalms teach us not just what God has done, but how to respond to him. Psalm 8 is the first Psalm we will read together, and it is fitting: it picks up exactly where the last three days have left us, meditating on the same creation and the same dignity of humanity that Genesis 1-2 described.
observation: The psalm opens and closes with the same line: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth.” This is called an inclusio, it frames the whole psalm in worship.
Babies and infants are mentioned in verse 2 as the means by which God establishes strength against his enemies. Strength comes from unexpected places in God’s economy.
The psalm moves from the cosmic (the heavens, the moon, the stars) to the personal (what is man that you are mindful of him?) and back to the cosmic.
The question “what is man?” is asked in the middle of looking at the night sky. Smallness is felt; the answer comes anyway: humanity has been crowned with glory and honor.
Verses 6-8 echo Genesis 1:26-28, dominion over the works of God’s hands, all things under his feet.
interpretation:
Psalm 8 is David’s response to the same wonder that Genesis 1 and 2 set up. Looking at the night sky, David asks the question every honest person eventually asks: in this enormous universe, why does humanity matter? The stars are vast. The moon hangs distant and unchanging. Compared to the cosmos, a human being is small, fragile, and temporary. So why does God care?

David’s answer is not that humanity is, in fact, more impressive than it seems. It is that God has chosen to crown humanity with glory and honor. The dignity of humans is not earned, it is given. We have value because God has assigned us value, made us in his image, and given us responsibility over what he has made. Verse 6 directly echoes Genesis 1:28: “You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet.”

But the psalm has a depth that the New Testament will later uncover. When the writer of Hebrews quotes Psalm 8 in Hebrews 2, he applies it to Jesus. “You have crowned him with glory and honor”, yes, that is true of humanity in general, but it is most truly fulfilled in the one true human, the second Adam, who succeeded where the first Adam failed. Jesus is the man who actually fulfills the role Psalm 8 describes, the human under whose feet all things will finally be subjected. Already, Hebrews says, we see him “crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death.” The dignity of humanity, lost in Genesis 3, is recovered in Christ.

So Psalm 8 is both a celebration of the dignity God has given us and a confession of the wonder that God should bother with us at all. It is honest about smallness. The night sky humbles. But the smallness only makes the love of God more astonishing. He sees you. He knows your name. He has crowned you with glory and honor. This is the truth that Christianity proclaims against every philosophy that says humans are accidents and against every culture that reduces humans to their usefulness.
connection: For three days we have been reading Genesis, the creation, the garden, the fall. Psalm 8 is the appropriate response. It looks at what God has made and worships. It looks at what God has done for humanity and marvels. And it does so without yet knowing what we know, that the one truly crowned with glory and honor will be Jesus, the Son of David, in whom the dignity of humanity is finally restored. Pray this Psalm today as someone who knows the rest of the story.
application:
Read this Psalm again, slowly, as a prayer. When you reach the question “what is man that you are mindful of him?”, let yourself sit with both the smallness and the dignity. You are smaller than you think and more loved than you can imagine.

This week, look at the sky at night, if you can. Let it remind you of how vast God’s creation is, and let that vastness lead you to worship rather than despair. Then look at the people around you, your spouse, your children, the cashier at the store, the stranger in traffic, and remember that each of them has been crowned with glory and honor by God. The doctrine of human dignity is not a slogan; it is a practice. It changes how you treat the people God has made.

And finally, look at yourself. If you have ever wondered whether you matter, Psalm 8 answers you. The God who counts and names every star is mindful of you. The maker of galaxies cares about your life. You are not an accident, and you are not insignificant. You are an image-bearer crowned with glory by the Creator of all things, and in Christ that glory is being restored.
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 8 slowly, twice, and aloud if you can. It is short, only nine verses. Notice that it begins and ends with the same line, and notice the question in the middle: “What is man that you are mindful of him?” Let the psalm lead you to look at the night sky as the psalmist did.
prayerPrompts: Stand in wonder before God’s majesty, and tell him what stirs in you when you think of how small you are and how much he has given you.
Thank him that Christ restores the dignity Adam lost.
Ask him to help you see each person you meet today as crowned with honor.
